forces.title: Accelerating HVDC deployment for offshore wind transmission
forces.description: The accelerating deployment of High-Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) systems for offshore wind and urban grid connections is a significant tailwind. HVDC technology is crucial for efficiently transmitting bulk power from remote offshore wind farms to load centers, reducing network losses and supporting grid stability. This infrastructural advancement directly enables the expansion and integration of large-scale offshore wind generation, a key component of grid-connected renewables.
forces.source_title: The power conversion market: Decarbonization and growth opportunities

forces.title: Increased Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) deployment for grid stability
forces.description: The rapid deployment of utility-scale, grid-connected Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) is a crucial structural change and tailwind for renewable generation. As intermittent sources like solar and wind increase their share of energy supply, BESS helps address the heightened need for grid stability, improved capacity utilization, and flexible dispatch. This growth, projected to triple by 2030 in the power conversion equipment market for BESS, directly supports the reliable integration and monetization of renewable assets.
forces.source_title: The power conversion market: Decarbonization and growth opportunities

forces.title: Price pressure on solar PV inverter equipment compressing market size
forces.description: The market for power conversion technologies in utility-scale solar PV is projected to decline by 2 percent through 2030, largely due to intense price compression and increased competition among equipment manufacturers. This price pressure on critical components like inverters directly impacts the total cost of ownership for utility-scale solar PV projects, potentially compressing project margins for renewable generators. Compliance with grid codes and grid-stabilizing features become increasingly important amidst these economic pressures.
forces.source_title: The power conversion market: Decarbonization and growth opportunities

forces.title: More efficient integration of batteries and solar with hybrid AC/DC architectures
forces.description: The increasing adoption of hybrid AC/DC power architectures in various applications, driven by DC-native sources like solar PV and batteries, offers a significant upside. This architectural shift enables lower conversion losses, superior energy recuperation, and reduced copper requirements, leading to more efficient integration of renewable generation with storage. These improvements contribute to higher usable power density and reduced operating costs for facilities leveraging renewables, enhancing their overall economic viability.
forces.source_title: The Strategic Case for Hybrid AC/DC Power

forces.title: Workforce shortages for DC system installation constraining energy transition
forces.description: A significant key risk for the energy transition, drawing parallels with the early expansion of solar PV, is the insufficient availability of a qualified workforce with expertise in DC system architecture, protection, integration, and commissioning. While technology questions are largely answered, deployment can be constrained by a lack of skilled installers. This workforce gap could slow the adoption and integration of advanced power systems crucial for grid-connected renewables, potentially impacting project timelines and costs across Europe.
forces.source_title: The Strategic Case for Hybrid AC/DC Power

forces.title: Intermittency and decentralization increase grid complexity for renewables
forces.description: The fundamental shift towards more decentralized and intermittent renewable supply, with a multiplication of grid connection points, is creating increasing complexity in European power systems. This structural change widens the distance between generation and demand and creates temporal mismatches, posing a challenge for grid stability and efficient power delivery. The system's ability to absorb, move, store, and price electricity becomes a primary bottleneck, necessitating advanced grid management and flexibility solutions.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Growing renewable curtailment and negative pricing impact project viability
forces.description: European power markets are experiencing record volumes of voluntarily curtailed renewable power and increasingly frequent hours of negative pricing. In 2025, combined curtailment in Germany, France, and the Netherlands reached nearly 4 TWh, growing at an 18 percent CAGR since 2020. This trend, exacerbated by synchronized renewable generation peaks across regions and limited cross-border export options, directly leads to price cannibalization and impacts the commercial viability and revenue streams of grid-connected renewable energy projects, acting as a significant headwind.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Demand for greater grid capacity, storage, and flexibility to integrate renewables
forces.description: The build-out of intermittent renewables necessitates substantial investment in greater grid capacity, storage solutions, and flexibility to make clean power usable when and where needed. This includes battery energy storage systems, demand-side response, spatial optimization, and grid expansion. A rising premium is placed on solutions that can resolve grid congestion, temporal mismatches, and curtailment, indicating a fundamental shift in the market structure towards valuing assets that enhance system reliability and integration for renewables.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Diversification of generation ownership away from incumbents
forces.description: The ownership structure of generation capacity in Europe, particularly Germany, has diversified significantly. Incumbent utilities' share of installed capacity fell from 82% in 2000 to 26% by 2026, while Independent Power Producers (IPPs) grew to 41% and prosumers to 33%. This structural change indicates a more fragmented and competitive market for renewable generation investment, with traditional utilities prioritizing regulated grid infrastructure, and new entrants and large off-takers filling the generation capacity gap, altering the landscape for project development.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Rapid expansion of data centers driving electricity demand
forces.description: Europe's data center capacity is projected to nearly double from 20 GW in 2025 to almost 40 GW by 2030, creating a significant increase in electricity demand (approx. 450 TWh). This rapid expansion, fueled by AI and digitalization, is a major upside driver for renewable generation. It creates new requirements for orchestrated flexibility, on-site storage, and microgrid services, providing opportunities for renewable generators to secure firm supply contracts and integrate with these high-demand loads.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Increased EU binding renewable energy targets
forces.description: The European Union has raised its binding renewable energy sources (RES) target to at least 42.5 percent of final energy consumption by 2030 (from 32 percent) and set a target of 60 GW of installed offshore wind capacity by 2030. These ambitious targets represent a strong policy tailwind for grid-connected renewable generation, providing a clear mandate for accelerated deployment and investment across Europe to reduce dependence on imported fuels and improve system resilience, despite implementation challenges.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Surging costs, supply chain bottlenecks, and unfavorable auction designs hinder deployment
forces.description: A significant key risk is the cooling developer appetite for renewable projects due to a combination of surging capital costs, persistent supply chain bottlenecks, and unfavorable auction designs. This friction is evident in recent failures of offshore wind auctions in Germany (2.5 GW without bids in August 2025) and the Netherlands (1 GW Nederwiek I-A site in late 2025). These factors challenge the economic viability of new projects, potentially delaying the deployment necessary to meet ambitious EU renewable targets.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: EU policies driving supply chain resilience and domestic clean tech manufacturing
forces.description: European Union industrial policies, such as the Net-Zero Industry Act (NZIA) and Critical Raw Materials Act (CRMA), represent a structural shift towards greater supply chain resilience and diversification. NZIA targets 40% domestic manufacturing capacity for clean technologies by 2030, while CRMA aims to reduce import dependence on critical raw materials. This focus can de-risk the supply chain for renewable generation projects by fostering local production, although it might also lead to higher component costs compared to global sourcing.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Increased EU scrutiny on non-European renewable component suppliers
forces.description: In the first half of 2026, the European Union increased scrutiny of Chinese participation in critical energy infrastructure, including restricting EU funding for renewable energy projects that utilize inverters from 'high-risk' suppliers. This reflects a broader strategic shift from pure cost optimization towards supply chain resilience and strategic autonomy. Such measures act as a headwind for renewable generators by potentially limiting access to cost-competitive components, increasing procurement costs, or extending project timelines due to supply chain adjustments.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: EU shift to two-way Contracts for Difference (CfDs) for renewables
forces.description: The EU Electricity Market Design Reform of 2024 established two-way Contracts for Difference (CfDs) as the default support mechanism for new, publicly supported renewable projects. This structural change provides long-term revenue visibility and limits exposure to power price volatility for capital-intensive renewable energy infrastructure. By capping both upside and downside price exposure, CfDs encourage investment by offering greater financial certainty, directly benefiting grid-connected renewable generators seeking stable, infrastructure-like returns across Europe.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Accelerating capacity market reforms and regulated support in multiple EU countries
forces.description: European member states, including Belgium, France, Italy, Ireland, and Greece, are rapidly accelerating capacity market reforms and increasing regulated support for energy assets. This trend enhances investment visibility and revenue predictability for low-carbon generation like offshore wind and storage, aiming to support system adequacy and flexibility. These mechanisms reduce reliance on pure merchant exposure and wholesale market volatility, providing a significant tailwind for grid-connected renewable generators by offering more stable and predictable revenue streams.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: Grid constraints limiting renewable integration in Ireland
forces.description: Ireland's energy sector continues to face challenges from grid constraints, which pose a key risk for the seamless integration and dispatch of new renewable generation capacity. As the country aims to expand its domestic renewable footprint to reduce high import dependence, existing grid limitations can create bottlenecks, leading to potential curtailment or delays in connecting new projects. This necessitates significant investment in grid upgrades and flexibility solutions to unlock the full potential of grid-connected renewables.

forces.title: Energy security drive due to high import dependence in Ireland
forces.description: Ireland's high energy import dependence (approximately 80%) and continued reliance on fossil fuels, particularly gas, create a strong strategic imperative for expanding domestic energy sources. Geopolitical energy shocks and price volatility underscore the need for greater energy security. This political and economic driver acts as a significant tailwind for grid-connected renewable generation, as it provides a compelling rationale for accelerated investment and deployment of indigenous renewable capacity to enhance national energy independence and resilience.

viewpoints.title: Growth in supply-side renewable energy sources is projected to slow down
viewpoints.description: McKinsey projects that the growth in supply-side renewable energy applications, such as solar PV, is expected to slow down with a CAGR decline of 2 percent from 2024 to 2030. This moderation is attributed to the market maturing over the past few decades, in contrast to the rapid growth seen in demand-side applications like data centers and EVs. The trend suggests a more tempered outlook for the expansion of raw renewable generation capacity compared to previous periods.
viewpoints.source_title: The power conversion market: Decarbonization and growth opportunities

viewpoints.title: Europe's renewable challenge shifts from capacity to usability and grid integration
viewpoints.description: McKinsey argues that Europe's primary challenge for clean power has evolved beyond merely expanding generation capacity to ensuring power is usable, connected, and flexible. The increasing intermittency and decentralization of renewable sources, coupled with multiplying grid connection points, are creating complexity. The focus must now be on solving bottlenecks related to the system's ability to absorb, move, store, and price electricity, rather than just adding raw megawatts, implying a more nuanced approach to renewable deployment.
viewpoints.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

viewpoints.title: Traditional utilities' retreat from generation creates opportunities for new entrants
viewpoints.description: McKinsey observes that traditional utilities are increasingly retreating from direct investment in generation capacity, including renewables, due to the more predictable economics of regulated grid infrastructure. This strategic shift creates a capacity gap that is likely to be filled by independent power producers (IPPs), new entrants, and non-traditional actors, such as large off-takers like data centers seeking dedicated firm supply. This could lead to a more diversified and competitive renewable generation landscape in Europe.
viewpoints.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

viewpoints.title: EU renewable targets may not be met without regulatory and financial restructuring
viewpoints.description: McKinsey expresses concern that the European Union's ambitious renewable energy targets may not be achieved without significant regulatory and financial restructuring. Despite strong policy intentions, surging capital costs, supply chain bottlenecks, and unfavorable auction designs have cooled developer appetite, leading to notable failures in recent offshore wind bidding rounds in Germany and the Netherlands. This highlights a gap between policy ambition and market reality, necessitating intervention to ensure targets are met.
viewpoints.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

viewpoints.title: Evolving regulatory frameworks are enhancing profitability and investment visibility for renewables
viewpoints.description: McKinsey indicates that European policymakers are increasingly adopting long-term support mechanisms, such as two-way Contracts for Difference (CfDs) and capacity markets, to encourage investment in capital-intensive energy infrastructure. This shift, formalized by the EU Electricity Market Design Reform of 2024, aims to limit exposure to power price volatility and improve investment visibility, making regulated and policy-backed revenues more prominent. This trend enhances the attractiveness and profitability for grid-connected renewable generation projects.
viewpoints.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

viewpoints.title: Ireland's energy sector stable but challenged by fossil fuel dependence and grid constraints
viewpoints.description: Allianz Ireland assesses the country's energy sector as broadly stable, yet vulnerable due to high import dependence (approximately 80%) and continued reliance on fossil fuels, particularly gas. The sector faces ongoing challenges from geopolitical energy shocks and grid constraints. However, state-backed operators like ESB and EirGrid benefit from regulated revenue streams, providing a degree of insulation. This dynamic suggests continued pressure for domestic, diversified energy supply, including renewables, to enhance security.
